connection: Employee exists, and ClockEntryRepository demonstrates List storage. Employees still have no production lookup component. Create an in-memory EmployeeRepository with dictionary lookup and deliberate name uniqueness.
objectives: Explain why Dictionary<int, Employee> gives EmployeeDirectory faster lookup by EmployeeId than scanning a List<Employee> would.
Trace TryAdd's role in Dictionary<TKey,TValue>: what happens when Add is called with a key that already exists, versus TryAdd.
Explain why EmployeeDirectory's Cities field is a HashSet<string>, not a List<string> -- what guarantee a set provides that a list does not.
Predict TryFind's return value and out parameter for both a present and an absent EmployeeId.

visuals.title: Dictionary<int, Employee> keys by EmployeeId
visuals.explanation: employees.TryAdd(employee.EmployeeId, employee) stores each Employee under its own id -- looking one up later means a direct key lookup, not scanning every entry.

visuals.title: TryAdd refuses to overwrite an existing key
visuals.explanation: employees.TryAdd(1, second) returns false if EmployeeId 1 is already present -- the original Employee stays in the dictionary, untouched.

visuals.title: HashSet<string> stores each city name once
visuals.explanation: cities.Add("Springfield") followed by cities.Add("Springfield") again leaves Cities.Count unchanged -- a set silently ignores a duplicate add.

visuals.title: TryFind mirrors the Try-pattern from Session 9
visuals.explanation: bool TryFind(int employeeId, out Employee? employee) returns whether the id was found, with employee assigned either way.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does EmployeeDirectory use Dictionary<int, Employee> instead of List<Employee> for its main storage?
options: Looking up an Employee by EmployeeId is a direct key lookup in a Dictionary, versus scanning every element in a List until a match is found
Dictionary is required by the Employee class
List<Employee> cannot hold more than a fixed number of items
preQuiz.explanation: A Dictionary trades a small amount of memory overhead for average constant-time lookup by key -- exactly the operation TryFind needs to perform quickly.

preQuiz.prompt: What does employees.TryAdd(1, secondEmployee) return if EmployeeId 1 is already stored?
options: false -- TryAdd never overwrites an existing key; the dictionary keeps the first Employee it was given for that id
preQuiz.explanation: TryAdd is specifically designed to fail gracefully (returning false) on a duplicate key, rather than throwing (like Add would) or silently overwriting.

preQuiz.prompt: After cities.Add("Springfield") twice in a row, what is Cities.Count?
options: 1 -- HashSet<string> silently ignores an Add call for a value it already contains
preQuiz.explanation: A set's defining guarantee is that each distinct value appears at most once -- Add returns false on a duplicate but does not throw or change the set's contents.

concept.title: Dictionary<int, Employee>: lookup by key, not by scanning
paragraphs: EmployeeDirectory's private Dictionary<int, Employee> employees maps each EmployeeId directly to its Employee -- TryFind's employees.TryGetValue(employeeId, out employee) is a direct key lookup, with no need to inspect every stored Employee.

Add uses employees.TryAdd(employee.EmployeeId, employee), returning false (and adding nothing) if that EmployeeId is already present -- this is what makes Add's own return value meaningful as a duplicate-detection signal.

concept.title: HashSet<string>: membership, not order or count
paragraphs: cities is a HashSet<string>, chosen specifically because EmployeeDirectory only ever needs to answer 'which distinct cities are represented' -- not 'in what order were they added' or 'how many employees are in each city.'
Adding the same city twice (from two different employees) is expected and harmless: HashSet.Add returns false for the second call and the set's contents are unchanged.

concept.title: TryFind: the out-pattern from Session 9, applied to a real lookup
paragraphs: TryFind(int employeeId, out Employee? employee) reuses exactly the pattern Session 9 introduced with TryGetOpenEntry -- a bool result plus an out parameter, so callers can check 'was this employee found' without a nullable-return null check.
TryGetValue on Dictionary<TKey,TValue> is itself built on the same Try-pattern -- EmployeeDirectory's TryFind is a thin wrapper exposing that same idiom at the EmployeeDirectory level.
concept.code: public bool TryFind(int employeeId, out Employee? employee) => employees.TryGetValue(employeeId, out employee);

lab.objective: Create an in-memory EmployeeRepository with dictionary lookup and deliberate name uniqueness.
lab.startingCondition: Employee exists, and ClockEntryRepository demonstrates List storage. The main application code does not yet have an employee lookup component.
steps: Create EmployeeRepository.cs in the Domain project's Repositories folder.
Declare the public sealed EmployeeRepository class.

Side note — sealed means this concrete in-memory repository cannot be used as a base class. Use sealed when a class is intended to be used as-is and you have not designed a safe inheritance contract with protected or virtual extension points. It is not required for every repository. Later, alternative storage implementations will implement a repository interface instead of inheriting from this class.

steps.text: Inside the class, declare a private readonly dictionary keyed by EmployeeId. The field initializer gives every repository object its own dictionary.
Declare a private readonly set for employee names. OrdinalIgnoreCase makes names that differ only by letter casing count as duplicates.
Stub TryAdd first. Its bool reports success, while message explains the result to the caller.
Stub TryFind with the Try-pattern from Session 09. Employee? is nullable because the requested ID might not exist.
Build the solution before implementing either method. A successful build confirms the fields and method contracts compile.

steps: Replace the throw in TryAdd with a check that returns false and assigns a duplicate-name message when _employeeNames already contains employee.Name.
After the name check, call _employees.TryAdd using employee.EmployeeId as the key and employee as the value.
When TryAdd returns false, assign a duplicate-ID message and return false.
After both duplicate checks succeed, add employee.Name to _employeeNames.
Assign a success message and return true from TryAdd.
Replace the throw in TryFind by returning _employees.TryGetValue(employeeId, out employee).
At the end of App/Program.cs, create a new Session 12 section without deleting the earlier application workflow.
In the new App section, create one valid employee and add it through TryAdd.
Attempt to add another employee with the same ID and display the rejection message.
Attempt to add another employee whose name differs only by casing and display the rejection message.
Call TryFind with the stored ID and display the employee when it is found.
Call TryFind with a missing ID and confirm that it returns false and assigns null to the out variable.

commit: session-11: teach dictionaries sets and lookup semantics
review: The lab uses production because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.
Earlier production code, tests, and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: If EmployeeDirectory used List<Employee> instead of Dictionary<int, Employee>, what would TryFind have to do differently?
options: Scan the list checking each Employee's EmployeeId until a match is found or the list ends -- an O(n) search instead of Dictionary's average O(1) key lookup
Nothing -- List<Employee> supports the exact same TryFind signature with no behavior change
TryFind would no longer be possible
postQuiz.explanation: The performance and simplicity difference is the entire reason Dictionary was chosen -- a List-based TryFind is a linear search hidden behind the same-looking method signature.

postQuiz.prompt: Why is cities.Add("Springfield") safe to call every time an Employee is added, even for a city already present?
options: HashSet<string>.Add is idempotent for values already present -- it returns false and changes nothing, rather than throwing or duplicating the entry
It is not safe -- calling Add on an existing value throws an exception
postQuiz.explanation: This is precisely why HashSet was chosen over List for Cities -- the caller never has to check 'is this city already here' before adding.

postQuiz.prompt: What would change about EmployeeDirectory.Add's duplicate-EmployeeId behavior if Dictionary's Add method were used instead of TryAdd?
options: Add(employee.EmployeeId, employee) would throw an ArgumentException on a duplicate key, instead of TryAdd's graceful false return -- EmployeeDirectory.Add would need a try/catch to match its current behavior
Nothing -- Add and TryAdd behave identically on a duplicate key
The dictionary would silently overwrite the existing entry
postQuiz.explanation: Dictionary<TKey,TValue>.Add throws on a duplicate key; TryAdd was specifically chosen so EmployeeDirectory.Add can return false instead of needing exception handling for an expected, everyday outcome (Session 24's throw-vs-return rule, applied here).

reflections.question: Where else in this codebase might a List currently used for something a Dictionary would serve better, or vice versa?
reflections.answer: ClockEntryRepository needs multiple chronological entries per employee, so one flat List remains reasonable for append-and-filter behavior. If repeated lookup by employee became a measured bottleneck, a Dictionary<int, List<ClockEntry>> could group entries by EmployeeId. Conversely, a Dictionary is unnecessary when order, duplicates, and sequential processing are the actual requirements.

reflections.question: Why does EmployeeDirectory.Add check the return value of TryAdd before deciding whether to add the city to Cities?
reflections.answer: TryAdd returns false when the EmployeeId already exists. Adding the city only after success keeps Cities consistent with employees that were actually accepted. If the city were added first, a rejected duplicate employee could introduce a city that no stored employee represents.

reflections.question: How does TryFind's Try-pattern connect back to what Session 9 taught about out parameters?
reflections.answer: TryFind returns a Boolean indicating success and assigns the found Employee through an out parameter. The compiler requires that out value to be assigned on every return path. This is the same success-plus-additional-result shape introduced in Session 9 and used by Dictionary.TryGetValue itself.

whatBreaks: Replacing TryAdd with Add in EmployeeDirectory.Add would turn a duplicate-EmployeeId scenario from a handled, expected outcome (false return) into an unhandled ArgumentException, violating the throw-vs-return distinction Session 24 establishes. Replacing HashSet<string> with List<string> for Cities would let the same city accumulate duplicate entries every time a new employee from that city is added, silently inflating Cities.Count. Removing StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase from the HashSet constructor would let differently-cased city names count as distinct cities again.
summary: EmployeeDirectory's Dictionary<int, Employee> gives TryFind fast lookup by EmployeeId, using TryAdd to reject duplicate keys gracefully instead of throwing. Its HashSet<string> Cities field guarantees each city name appears at most once, complementing Session 10's case-insensitive comparer choice. TryFind itself directly reuses the out-parameter Try-pattern Session 9 introduced.
